I follow the news quite carefully as a concerned, patriotic individual.  I note that the proposed regulation is fundamentally flawed in that at 17.272 (a)(58) it creates the misleading false impression that physicians are completely free, without pressure or constraint or fear of burdensome reprisal, to make the decision that the abortion is medically necessary.  There is ample case history where states have imposed similar regulations, and physicians then feel compelled to wait to make such a determination until no one could possibly contradict their determination -- and this leads to needless cruel pain and suffering, and in some cases actual death of the mother or permanent injuries.  (https://www.perplexity.ai/search/list-cases-where-women-were-in-4GdITr1iSMW0K_lsTPl87g)

 In addition, some states have gone to extraordinary lengths to investigate and prosecute doctors to intimidate them.  (https://www.perplexity.ai/search/list-cases-of-state-abortion-r-0z_P_unyRsCAcBYsUuoqmw)

This regulation is therefore defective in that it provides insufficient clarity to the freedom and authority of each physician to make the determination without challenge, and as such, promotes over-compliance out of fear, and put women's lives and fertility in jeopardy.  It misleads to create the impression that women will not be harmed because the decision of the physician will protect them, while the regulation does nothing to actually ensure that physicians are clearly in a position to to exercise that authority.

To remedy these defects, (1) the regulation should make clear that it intends to prohibit ELECTIVE abortion (versus the current wording of "full exclusion"); (2) the regulation should make clear the authority of individual physicians and the intent to indemnify them and protect them from Federal or State challenges to their determinations; (3) make clear whether or not the determination is limited to only certain select physicians (versus the physician of the individual's choice); (4) make clear how VA physicians will be instructed and regulated with respect to this provision; (5) make clear what provisions are made for an affected service member to get a "second opinion" if the VA physician's opinion seems to them in error; and (6) what procedures will be in place to make whole those women who suffer pain, loss of fertility, or death due to a delay or refusal by a VA physician to make the determination.

Furthermore, however, the intent to regulate elective abortions is fundamentally flawed in that military rules dictate the state in which a service member will serve, and the incidence of sexual assault is a major problem (https://www.perplexity.ai/search/provide-statistics-on-sexual-a-vUrVpkwARQivVz9Q6JPrKA).  It is a disservice and a denial of individual civil rights to mandate the location of a person to a place where they do not have rights.  As long as states are allowed to prohibit elective abortions, the VA ought to do so until it has regulated its sexual assault problem to zero.

Here are the key statistics and insights on sexual assault in the United States military based on
the most recent data from 2024 and 2025:
Overall, while reported sexual assault numbers in the U.S. military show a modest decline
recently, independent studies indicate the true prevalence is much higher, and continued efforts
are underway to improve prevention, reporting, and accountability across all service branches.
⁂
provide statistics on sexual assault in the military
of the United States.
In 2024, there were 8,195 reported sexual assaults in the military, down about 4% from
8,515 in 2023. This indicates a second consecutive year of overall decline in reported cases.
Of these, 6,973 service members reported being assaulted during their military service, plus
512 reported assaults prior to joining the military. The Army saw the largest decrease with a
13% drop, while Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps saw slight increases. [1] [2] [3]
Despite official reports, independent research suggests the actual number of sexual assaults
is likely two to four times higher than the Department of Defense (DoD) estimates. For
example, in 2021, independent estimates showed over 75,500 incidents, compared to the
DoD estimate of about 35,900. Similarly, estimated cases in 2023 were about 73,600, much
higher than the DoD’s reported 29,000. [4] [5]
The prevalence of sexual assault among active duty members is notable: around 6.8% of
women and 1.3% of men indicated experiencing a sexual assault or unwanted sexual
contact in the past year (2023), which corresponds to around 29,000 service members. [6]
Reporting rates are gradually improving—reporting of sexual assault increased from 20% in
2021 to 25% in fiscal year 2023, indicating more victims are coming forward, although
many assaults remain unreported. [6]
Efforts to address sexual assault include significant investments in prevention and response
programs, with over 1,400 trained prevention specialists deployed and plans to increase this
workforce. Legislation such as the "I Am Vanessa Guillén Act" has reformed the
investigative process by moving the authority over sexual assault cases out of the military
chain of command to independent prosecutors. [5] [1] [4]
Sexual harassment reports have risen slightly even as sexual assault reports declined,
highlighting ongoing challenges. [2] [3]

===== FILE 14488__2.pdf =====
Here are several documented cases and reports where women were injured due to medical
professionals hesitant or unable to determine that an abortion was necessary under restrictive
abortion laws:
These cases illustrate how abortion bans and ambiguous laws create hesitation among medical
professionals, leading to serious injury and trauma for pregnant women who need timely abortion
care to save their health or lives. Many have had to travel long distances or face life-threatening
complications as a result.
⁂
list cases where women were injured due to
medical professionals hesitant to determine
abortion was necessary
Mylissa Farmer experienced permanent physical and emotional damage after two hospitals
in Missouri and Kansas refused to provide abortion care despite her water breaking
prematurely and risk of serious infection. She had to travel four hours in labor to receive
necessary care. The federal government found these hospitals violated emergency care
laws by denying the abortion. [1] [2]
Amanda from Texas nearly died of sepsis after her water broke at 18 weeks, and doctors,
constrained by vague Texas abortion laws, hesitated to induce labor or terminate the
pregnancy even though the fetus had no chance of survival. [3] [4]
Kyleigh Thurman from Texas was sent home from the emergency department bleeding and
in pain with a potentially deadly ectopic pregnancy, but doctors refused to treat her under
the abortion ban. [2]
Meagan in Wisconsin, who had multiple pregnancy complications including a life-threatening
placenta previa and fetal anomaly, was unable to get an abortion without approval from
three doctors. Despite doctors agreeing the pregnancy risked her life, no hospital was
willing to perform the procedure, forcing her to seek care out of state. [5]
The Texas Supreme Court refused to clarify the "medical emergency" exceptions in
abortion bans, leaving doctors uncertain and causing harm to pregnant women who were
denied abortions despite facing dangerous complications. Twenty women brought lawsuits
describing denied care that resulted in risks to their health, fertility, and lives. [6] [7]
Sepsis, permanent damage to reproductive organs, forced travel for care, near fatal
infections, and emotional trauma have been common outcomes in documented cases where
doctors hesitated or were legally restricted from determining or acting on the necessity of
abortion care. [4] [1] [3] [5] [6]

===== FILE 14488__3.pdf =====
Cases of state abortion regulations threatening out-of-state doctors involve legal actions
primarily against providers who prescribe or provide abortion-inducing medication to patients in
states that ban or restrict abortion.
Key cases include:
These examples reflect ongoing conflicts between states with abortion bans and out-of-state
providers in states with protective laws.
⁂
list cases of state abortion regulations
threatening out-of-state doctors
A civil case in Texas against a New York physician who prescribed abortion medication via
telehealth to a Texas resident. Texas sued for practicing medicine without Texas licensure
and aiding abortion in violation of Texas law, seeking injunction, fines, and attorney fees.
A criminal case in Louisiana against the same New York physician for violating Louisiana’s
abortion ban by providing abortive care to a resident through telemedicine.
These cases exemplify the risk out-of-state providers face, including loss of licensure and
legal liabilities for providing abortion care to patients in restrictive states.
New York and other states have enacted shield laws to protect providers physically located
within those states from out-of-state prosecutions and disciplinary actions.
The Texas case led to a court enjoining the physician from prescribing to Texan residents
and ordering payment of a $100,000 civil fine.
Legislation and legal battles continue over issues like the anonymization of prescription
labels to shield doctors from being targeted by restrictive states.
